title: Can, want, must
goal: Expressing ability, wishes, obligation and permission — four things that stop your sentences sounding like a list of facts.
bekal: say what you can, want to, must and may do
use *-маар байна* for a wish you feel right now

dialogs.title: Яриа — Гэрт урих
dialogs.intro: Sarnai invites Budi to dinner at her family's home. Budi wants to come, but there are a few things he needs to check first.

lines.speaker: Сарнай:
lines.id: Budi, can you come to our place on Saturday?
lines.literal: Budi, Saturday-on our-at come-ing may Q?

lines.speaker: Буди:
lines.id: Of course! I'd really like to go. What time should I be there?
lines.literal: of-course! I arrive-want is. what hour-at arrive must Q?

lines.speaker: Сарнай:
lines.id: Seven o'clock. Coming earlier is fine too.
lines.literal: seven hour-at. early come-ing also may.

lines.speaker: Буди:
lines.id: What should I bring? I'd like to bring something.
lines.literal: what bring must Q? I thing bring-want is.

lines.speaker: Сарнай:
lines.id: You don't need to bring anything. But if you want, you can bring fruit.
lines.literal: what even bring need-not. but if-want fruit bring-ing may.

lines.speaker: Буди:
lines.id: OK. Can I manage in Mongolian? Does your mother speak English?
lines.literal: OK. I Mongolian-in speak-ing able probably Q? your mother English-in speak-usually Q?

lines.speaker: Сарнай:
lines.id: My mother doesn't speak English. But you speak well, you know.
lines.literal: our mother English-in speak-ing able-usually-not. but you well speak-ing able you-know.

lines.speaker: Буди:
lines.id: I'm nervous. I might make mistakes.

lines.speaker: Сарнай:
lines.id: Don't be afraid. You're supposed to make mistakes — that's how you learn.
lines.literal: don't fear. mistake put-out must, so learn.

lines.speaker: Буди:
lines.id: True. Do I have to take my shoes off when I go in?
lines.literal: true. house-into enter-when-own shoe-own take-off must Q?

lines.speaker: Сарнай:
lines.id: Yes. And you mustn't step on the threshold.
lines.literal: yes. also threshold on step-ing may-not you-know.

lines.speaker: Сарнай:
lines.id: By old custom, the threshold is the guardian of the home. Stepping on it is disrespectful.
lines.literal: old custom-with threshold as-for house's guardian. if-step respect-not so say.

lines.speaker: Буди:
lines.id: I see, good thing you told me. What else should I know?
lines.literal: understood, good say-ing gave. other what know need Q?

lines.speaker: Сарнай:
lines.id: You must take the tea with both hands. That's all!
lines.literal: tea-object two hand-with take must. then enough!

notes: ⚠️ **Four patterns, four words, and all of them come AFTER the main verb** — because the main verb itself is at the end of the sentence. *Ярьж **чадна*** (can speak), *очих **ёстой*** (must go), *ирж **болно*** (may come), *очмоор **байна*** (want to go).

**Чадах = be able, and it needs the -ж / -ч form before it.** *Ярь**ж** чадна* = can speak. ⚠️ Don't mix it up with *болох*, which means "may, be allowed": *чадах* is about ability, *болох* about permission. Casual English uses "can" for both, so this is a split you need to build from scratch.

**Ёстой = must, and it needs the dictionary form (-х) before it.** *Очих ёстой* = must go. For "don't need to", use *шаардлагагүй* or *хэрэггүй*; for "mustn't", use *болохгүй*. ⚠️ All three are different: *ёстой биш* is rarely used.

**-маар байна means "want to" as felt right now.** *Очмоор байна* = I feel like going. Compare *хүсэх*, which is more formal and about bigger wishes: *Би эмч болохыг хүсэж байна* = I want to become a doctor.

**Орохдоо uses the -хдаа / -хдээ suffix, meaning "when, while".** *Гэрт **орохдоо*** = when entering the house. It's a very useful form you'll hear often; it's covered fully at A2, but learn to recognize it now because it shows up everywhere.

grammars.title: Four patterns and the form that comes before them
body: What matters is not the meaning but **which form has to come before it**. Three patterns take the *-ж / -ч* form, one takes the dictionary form *-х*. Memorize the pairs, not the words on their own.
after: ⚠️ **The negative goes on the second word, not on the main verb.** *Ярьж **чадахгүй*** (can't speak), *явах **ёсгүй*** (shouldn't go), *орж **болохгүй*** (mustn't come in). The main verb stays as it is.

**To ask permission, the most polite form is *… болох уу?*** — and it pairs with any verb. If you memorize only one pattern from this unit, make it this one: it opens doors in shops, offices and people's homes.

grammars.title: Making -маар байна
body: From the dictionary form, drop *-х*, add **-маар / -мээр / -моор / -мөөр** following vowel harmony, then *байна*.
after: **The negative: *-маар байхгүй*, or more often *… хүсэхгүй байна*.** In conversation people prefer a softer, positive-sounding refusal: *Одоо биш* (not now), *Дараа* (later), *Болих байх* (maybe I'll pass).

⚠️ There's one more form to recognize because it's often used for invitations: **-ъя / -ье / -ё**, meaning "let's". *Явъя* (let's go), *идье* (let's eat), *уулзая* (let's meet). It's only for the first person — you and the person you're talking to.

blocks.title: Declining an invitation without offending
items: *Уучлаарай, тэр өдөр завгүй байна.* — Sorry, I'm busy that day.
*Их баярлалаа, гэхдээ болохгүй нь.* — Thank you so much, but I don't think I can.
*Дараагийн удаад заавал очно.* — Next time I'll definitely come.
⚠️ Turning down a dinner invitation in Mongolia needs **a reason and a promise for next time**. A one-word "no" sounds like a rejection of the person, not of the event.

head: Монгол
English
rows: You should go to bed early.
You need to sort out a visa.
There's no need to do anything.
I want to become a doctor.

blocks.text: ⚠️ Look at the third row: **an ability that's an established skill uses *чаддаг*, not *чадна*.** *Морь унаж чаддаг* = "can ride a horse" as a skill you have. *Морь унаж чадна* sounds more like "is able to ride a horse (right now)". The difference is like "she can swim" versus "she can manage the swim today".

sections.title: A guest in a Mongolian home

blocks.text: This unit touches on something bigger than grammar: **Mongolian hospitality is among the most heartfelt in the world**, and it has rules that aren't written down anywhere. They come from life on the steppe, where turning a guest away could mean leaving someone to freeze.

head: What to do
Why
rows: **Accept anything offered with your right hand**, supported at the elbow by your left.
The left hand alone suggests you think little of it.
**Taste the tea or milk you're offered**, even just a sip.
Refusing it outright means refusing the home.
In old belief, the threshold guards the home.
**Don't point at the fire or throw rubbish into the hearth.**
Fire is the spirit of the household, the most revered of all.
**If you accidentally bump someone's foot, shake hands at once.**
A handshake cancels the slip instantly.
The sun's direction; the opposite way is thought to reverse your luck.
**The west side is for men and guests, the east side for women and the kitchen.**
The layout of the ger has been fixed for centuries.

blocks.text: One last thing to prepare for mentally: **if you're invited to eat, you'll be served more than you can finish, and saying no will be taken as mere politeness.** The most polite way out is to accept a little, praise the taste, and slow down gradually — just like at a grandparent's house. The lifesaving sentence: *Маш амттай байна, гэхдээ би цатгалан боллоо.*
